original_value: Traffic load in any 802.11 infrastructure mode network is typically distributed unevenly between access points (APs), creating hotspots. This is due to the inherent nature of wireless area networks (WLANs), where stations are free to associate to any known AP they desire, and the lack of control by the APs themselves. This imbalance creates a condition where affected APs in the network suffer traffic congestion while others are underutilized, leading to stations experiencing lower throughput, longer latency, and operating below the network potential capacity. To alleviate this problem, some form of load balancing is required to redistribute the work load among other available APs in the wireless network. This article presents a survey of the various works done in performing load balancing in an infrastructure mode wireless network and will cover the common methods including admission control, association management, cell breathing, and association control. Updates to the IEEE standards are also presented that support load-balancing efforts. Finally, software-defined networks are investigated to determine the extent of control integration to support managing and load-balancing WLANs. Trends in load-balancing research are also uncovered that indicate how the introduction of new wireless standards influences the amount of research.

result.paraphrase: In 802.11 infrastructure-mode networks, traffic is usually unevenly spread across access points (APs), which creates hotspots. This stems from the nature of wireless local area networks (WLANs), where stations may associate with any AP they know and where APs themselves have little control. The resulting imbalance leaves some APs congested while others are underused, causing lower throughput, higher latency, and operation below the network’s potential capacity. To address this issue, traffic must be redistributed among the available APs through load balancing. This article surveys the work on load balancing in infrastructure-mode wireless networks, covering common approaches such as admission control, association management, cell breathing, and association control. It also presents IEEE standard updates that support load-balancing efforts. Finally, it examines software-defined networks to assess the degree of control integration available for managing and balancing WLANs, and identifies research trends showing how new wireless standards affect the volume of load-balancing research.
